discovery: Discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and the opening of neutrino astronomy with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory
motivation: Francis Halzen conceived and led the construction of IceCube, a cubic-kilometre neutrino telescope in the Antarctic ice that grew out of the AMANDA pioneering effort. In 2013 IceCube reported the first flux of high-energy neutrinos of extraterrestrial origin, a new window on the universe. It then identified the first sources: the blazar TXS 0506+056 (2018, in coincidence with gamma-ray observations), the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 (2022), and neutrino emission from the Galactic plane (2023). Like the dark-energy discovery, this result came from building an entirely new observational capability and following it through with statistical care against large atmospheric backgrounds. Neutrino astronomy now stands beside photons, cosmic rays and gravitational waves as a messenger of the high-energy universe and a probe of fundamental neutrino physics at energies far beyond accelerators. Halzen's vision and sustained scientific leadership were decisive for this achievement.
